ADVR300
Advertising Theory &
Practice
3
Advertising Theory and Practice provides a comprehensive overview on Advertising, its
role in building a brands image and brand equity, its diverse techniques used to
influence people's mind by satisfying or creating consumers needs, its communicational
impact on society that keeps on generating trends as well as its persuasive force in
increasing sales and encouraging consumers to make the purchase. Broad attention is
given to key subjects such as advertising agency practices, branding, media planning,
creative and marketing strategies.
ARTS350
Photography
3
Photography is addressed to all students who wish to learn about digital photography
basics, eventually, how to use a digital camera and lenses. Students will learn terms and
theory using manual techniques in a digital single lens reflex camera. This course
involves the power of images through image language, composition and philosophy. It
covers as well the use of the digital dark room for the enhancement of ideas, products
and /or creative necessity. It leads students towards a deeper understanding of light, key
value, equipment and camera controls
COMM200
Introduction to
Communication
Studies
3
Introduction to Mass Communication introduces students to the central concepts of
image theories in communication and the operation of the media industries. It is an
introduction to the history, structure, process and social environment of each medium in
the communication industry; an overview of the emerging technology in mass media and
its social impact. It is a study of the development, principles and effects of Print, Public
Relations, Advertising, Radio, TV, film and Computer/Online-Generated communication.
Particular attention will be given to the study of different types of mass and interactive
media and how they function in modern society. It reviews the historical and regulatory
bases of the media along with their social implications.
COMM220
Rhetoric & Persuasion
3
Rhetoric and Persuasion provides students with the foundation to understand the
definition of key terms, offering a retrospective glance to the historical foundations of
rhetoric and persuasion. It provides insights on important considerations of the
persuasion on the social through rhetoric. It provides a model for professional practice
focusing on developing skills in critical self-reflection, as well as professional persuasion.
COMM225
Workshop
3
Workshop I is an entry-level course that will introduce students to the fundamentals of
video making. Students will learn to use video and sound as an effective form of
communication, and will learn how to successfully utilize those elements separately and
simultaneously, to be able to transform an idea into a persuasive story.
COMM265
Performance Theory &
Practice
3
Performance Theory and Practice introduces students to the ambiguity that lies in trying
to define what performance as a discipline might mean, which makes this course very
challenging. It is very essential to note that performance in not theatre, without
neglecting the fact that performing is a part of acting. The subject in action is not an
actor; he is only experiencing a new game where others, as subjects (physical and
emotional) are taking part in this game. What comes out of this game is what will mark
the journey of each and every subject involved in this class. It is not a theatre course, but
it involves character games, breathing techniques, mediation and a rough body work.
And because the discipline is still under construction all around the world, the game
is set between the students and the facilitator. Hence, the facilitator i.e. the instructor
is part of the game. It is all about a behavior in front of an audience.
COMM285
Theories of Perception
3
Theories of Perception is an introductory course on communication languages and
perception modes in relation to the technology of image production. It is an investigation
of the semiotics of representation and perception throughout different medium usage
and major art and media movements. It also covers the development of image theories
and representation toward the various elements of communication and throughout
history in relation to technology as a major variable for the image production.
COMM305
Artificial Intelligence
and Mass Media
3
This course provides an in-depth exploration of the intersection between artificial
intelligence (AI) and mass media. It examines how AI technologies are transforming
media production, distribution, and consumption. Students will analyze the ethical
implications, the impact on journalism, advertising, and public relations, and the role of
AI in shaping societal narratives.
GDES270
Design Software I
3
Design software 1 introduces students to aiding software for Graphic Design. Using the
Adobe suite, Adobe Illustrator plays a significant role in graphic design. As a vector
oriented software, illustrator opens a gateway of opportunities for a graphic designer to
work with ease in implementing the essential work for print, web and other media.
Adobe InDesign complements Illustrator at producing multiple page content instead of
art boards and by that, playing an essential role at strengthening sense of layout and
identity. Adobe Photoshop plays a major role in photo editing. Accompanied by Adobe
illustrator, these 2 software manage to create most demanding projects especially that of
print. The student will have the opportunity to learn and practice the essentials in these
software. Keeping the sketchbook to bring up ideas to life, the designated software shall
add ease and speed rather than the long timed labor of manual work.
JORN285
Travel Journalism
3
Travel Journalism provides students with the foundation to understand the setting of the
fundamental writing skills required by freelance writers. It exposes students to the
experience and savoir-faire of successful travel writing. Flexible in its approach, the
course teaches the craft of creating travel media through writing and photography,
covering diverse topics of journalism and blogging. The objective is to address markets
needs through building skills in the chosen medium and creating and marketing the
writers personal brand.
PREL300
Public Relations
Principles & Concepts
3
Public Relations Principles and Concept introduces students to the basic principles of
public relations. In this course, students will learn how to identify the main concepts and
principles in the field of public relations, which will further be elaborated on, in
subsequent courses. The course will also provide students with the knowledge to
practice the basics of PR

CSCI200
Introduction to
Computers
3
This course introduces students to the fundamental concepts of computer science and
technology, with a focus on practical applications and interactive learning. Designed for
Generation Z students pursuing degrees in basic Education in English, Math, or Science,
the course emphasizes hands-on experience, critical thinking, and the use of modern
tools and platforms. The philosophy centers around fostering digital literacy and
responsible use of technology, recognizing the importance of equipping future educators
and professionals with essential tech skills. By the end of the course, students will be
proficient in using common software applications, understand basic computer hardware
and operating systems, and apply problem-solving skills to real-world scenarios using
computer tools. The impact of this course extends beyond technical proficiency, as it
aims to develop students' ability to navigate the digital world effectively, enhance their
educational and professional opportunities, and promote a culture of continuous learning
and adaptation in a rapidly evolving technological landscape.
CULT200
Introduction to Arab -
Islamic Civilization
3
This course delves into the intellectual and cultural achievements of Arab-Islamic
civilization, aiming to expose students to the significant contributions made by Arab
scholars in science, philosophy, literature, and the arts. Rooted in the philosophy that
open-minded inquiry fuels intellectual advancement, the course emphasizes the holistic
and curious approach of historical Arab scholars who transcended dogmatic limitations.
Through exploring these achievements, students will gain a broader perspective on the
development of global knowledge, recognizing the pivotal role of Arab-Islamic
civilization in connecting ancient and medieval worlds. By the end of the course,
students will appreciate the interconnectedness of human knowledge and be inspired to
adopt a spirit of curiosity and respect for diverse intellectual traditions in their pursuits.
The medium of instruction is in both English and Arabic.
ENGL201
Composition and
Research Skills
3
Welcome to the next step in your academic writing journey! This course marks an
advancement in students' academic writing development, focusing on the fundamental
skills of summarizing, paraphrasing, and synthesizing information. Building upon prior
English Language knowledge, the course aims to enhance students' critical thinking and
academic writing competencies. Students will engage with a diverse range of texts from
various disciplines, developing effective strategies for responding to and integrating
these sources within their written work. Through practical application, students will
focus on composing different essay forms, while also refining their ability to construct
clear, grammatically correct sentences and expanding their academic vocabulary and
diction. Upon completion of this course, students will be well-prepared to produce
thoroughly researched and synthesized essays, demonstrating their proficiency in
advanced academic writing.
ENGL251
Communication Skills
3
Thriving in todays fast-paced, digitally connected professional world requires strong and
adaptable communication abilities, making ENGL251  English Communication Skills an
essential foundation for career readiness. This course aims to develop students mastery
of key principles and strategies that underpin effective communication across various
professional scenarios. Rooted in the belief that communication proficiency grows
through both conceptual understanding and hands-on practice, the course blends
focused instruction with applied, real-world tasks. Students will explore audience
awareness and message design using the 3-X-3 writing process as a framework for
producing clear, purposeful communication. They will engage with topics such as
crafting persuasive and tactful negative messages, communicating professionally in
face-to-face settings, and enhancing their employability through the creation of
persuasive rsums, cover letters, and strong interview performance. Through a mix of
lectures, collaborative discussions, practical exercises, and digital writing assignments,
the course fosters an active and participatory classroom environment. Assessment
methods include quizzes, a midterm and final exam, as well as targeted business writing
tasks, ensuring students are evaluated on both theoretical insight and real-world
application. By the end of ENGL251, students will be well-equipped to communicate
confidently and effectively in a variety of digital and professional settings. They will be
able to tailor their messages to diverse audiences, engage in collaborative
communication, and use their English language skills strategically to succeed in the
modern workplace.
Major Requirements

Title
Credits
Description
COMM300
Media Laws & Ethics
3
Media Laws and Ethics introduces students to the major legal, ethical and policy issues
related to the media. This course will expose students to primary documents and cases
as well as to methods of analysis. It will examine freedom of expression and the
limitations imposed on such freedoms by statue and by common Law, and will provide
students with the foundation necessary to make ethical decisions within their profession
focusing on developing analysis techniques and applying them to ethical problems
through independent critical thinking and moral sensitivity.
COMM310
Research Methods in
Communication Arts
3
Research Methods in Communication Arts introduces students to the essentials of
conducting a research dealing with communication as a social science. Students will
learn how to identify a problem, ask questions and find answers through systematic
procedures from a Social Science perspective.
COMM320
Radio-TV Announcing
3
Radio/TV Announcing establishes the foundations to understand types of news and
delivery techniques. It provides insights on important considerations for vocal ability.
The course will expose and guide students to the techniques of delivering news texts
when producing quality journalism. It will provide a model for professional anchoring
focusing on developing skills in reading news with a self-ability to discover and correct
errors in pronunciation.
COMM330
Media Planning &
Audience Analysis
3
Media Planning and Audience Analysis introduces students to the cooperate todays
landscape. Students will learn the social order instituted by modernity, the identity of
organizations and the messages being communicated both externally and internally.
Students will also learn the importance of audience demographics, psychographics, and
product usage variables, which help to make creative media decisions in tune with the
changing marketplace.
COMM400
Media Management
3
Media management introduces students to the business of media. It allows them to
explore the uniqueness of information as a product, shedding the light on two
perspective models, namely the market one and that of the public sphere. While the
market aims at profits and the public sphere is concerned with public interest, facts,
theories and articles related to these issues, are communicated to the students.
JORN200
News Writing &
Reporting
3
News Writing and Reporting guides students with the foundation to understand the
definition of newsworthiness in journalism. It provides insights on important
considerations for sound decision-making about public interest, accuracy, and reliability
of sources. The course will expose and guide students to the processes and decisions
required when producing quality journalism. It provides a model for professional
practice focusing on developing skills in critical self-reflection, as well as professional
ethics.
JORN370
Arabic News Writing &
Reporting
3
Arab News Writing and Reporting provides students with the foundation to understand
journalistic writing style as a basic skill for all communication professions. The emphasis
is on basic news and writing skills which are useful for a career in print, broadcast, or
public relations. The course is intended to provide students with exposure and guidance
through the processes and decisions that are required when producing quality
journalism. It exposes students to the definition of newsworthy and considers decisions
about public interest, accuracy, and reliability of sources.
JORN375
Journalism Workshop
3
Journalism Workshop will provide students with the advanced journalism and multimedia
production skills needed to produce and report for news media (print and web-based).
Students will learn traditional reporting skills and techniques.
JORN380
Web Journalism
3
Web Journalism introduces new media as a growing phenomenon in journalism and
trains students to use its tools. It provides students with insights to be employed in their
future journalistic careers. The course will expose and guide students to learn how to
use and write for digital media. It provides a model for professional new-media themes,
such as the ethical and legal implications of publishing online, as well as the
characteristics that distinguish website news from print and broadcast media; guidelines
for doing proper research on the Internet are also covered.
JORN385
Citizen Journalism
3
Citizen Journalism guides students to understand and explore various forms and
functions of citizen journalism and considers how this new form of journalism can
complement or challenge traditional reporting. Students will produce content and work
with social media tools such as blogs and social media sites such as Twitter, Flickr, and
YouTube. Students who are considering a career in journalism or related fields, should
consider taking this course as should anyone interested in learning how to produce
digital media.
JORN410
News Production
3
News production is an introduction to the art and business of content production for
digital platforms. Concretely, the coursework emphasizes the differences between news
and feature writing, audience analysis, content promotion and fact checking. It aims to
give students a realistic and hands-on introduction into the complex process of creating
a digital news from scratch and the skills needed to do so. It aims to heighten students
creativity both in design and in writing. This course gives students experience in
conceptualizing, researching, and producing content for the digital. Ethical issues and
content creators relationships are also examined. The class will learn to discern a
mediums editorial style and readership as well as evaluate choices. Students are
empowered with the skills needed to create their own digital content, based on their
interests.
JORN440
Reporting of Public
Affairs
3
Reporting of Public Affairs explores covering local government, along with the aspects of
community life that fall under the general heading of public affairs. It discusses how
public policy decisions are reported. It focuses on beat reporting and advanced
assignments related to the legal, the social and the political news, such as: covering
budgets, public hearings, and community issues, as well as researching public records.
At the end of this course, students will be expected to demonstrate strong competence in
news judgment, reporting, and meeting deadlines. They will also have a basic
understanding of critical thinking for journalists and some familiarity with media ethics.
JORN450
Investigative
Journalism
3
Investigative Journalism is an introduction to the theory, the history and practice of
investigative Journalism. Students learn about the concept, the know-how, and the ethics
and will gain practical experience working collaboratively on an in-depth reporting
project. Investigative journalism as a tool for transparency and accountability rises the
following questions: Why it is a need nowadays? how this kind of journalism can be the
savior of traditional and professional journalism? Where to find stories and how to deal
with the sources? How to be ready for lawsuits? How to use the social media and the
web as a tool not as a threat? Furthermore, it discusses ethics, whistleblowing, and the
right of access to information.
JORN495
Senior Study in
Journalism
3
Senior Study in Journalism combines and demonstrates the knowledge and skills
acquired throughout the program with a comprehensive journalistic material that the
student produces. Through the weekly meetings, the instructor follows and makes sure
students will ultimately produce: a project for a media channel of their choice, its media
plan, academic research in journalism, and be prepared to defend their work in front of a
jury.
PREL455
Public Speaking
3
Public Speaking introduces students to the principles of public speaking; It critically
examines students own and others speeches through interactive practice. The course
introduces students to the essential of presentations, job interviews and in more general
instances of communication. It is an introduction to the rhetorical study dating back to
the Ancient Greeks, their structure and process of public speaking. It invites students to
critically examine their speeches as well as other students in addition to famous
speeches for formative purposes.
RATV316
Mobile Media
3
Mobile Media is an exploration of new video technologies involving digital photography
and portable video production, post-production and broadcast. It is a study of streaming
media for distribution on "hand- held" devices, "video casts" or "Podcast." Students from
Beirut Campus, Saida Campus, Nabatiyeh Campus and Tripoli Campus will all work
closely together in Beirut and another city of their choice to produce two video mapping
projects for each city.
RATV370
Writing for Radio and
TV
3
Writing for Radio and TV introduces students to the characteristics and rules for
effective writing for radio and TV while focusing on writing for simple news and reports.
The course teaches students the best ways to write for the ear in the case of writing for
radio, while focusing on the two levels that characterize such writing: Voice Over and
Natural Sound. As for writing for TV, it gives guidelines on how to write for the eye and
ear by using efficiently the four available levels: Picture, Voice Over, Natural Sounds and
Graphics.
RTVF425
Documentary Making
3
Documentary Making combines studies of existing recognized documentary films with
the creative exercise of the students own film production. This course is suitable for
both Radio/TV and Journalism students. The course will cover the history of documentary
filmmaking, and will encourage students to be aware of how each stylistic choice (of
framing, shot duration, shot scale, interview questions, camera angle, editing, lighting)
bears a history of both politics and art. The course will also focus on ethical problems,
research, reporting, interviewing, writing, legal issues, economics, aesthetics and
diversity of the documentary. In class discussions on established films will be very rich,
and students will consider the fine and changing balance between capturing a
spectators attention and sensationalizing a subject: how to tell stories and present
images/sounds that might make an audience feel and think? Finally, the course will also
focus on pre-production in the sense of a written script as students will go through script
writing for documentaries and the need for such a step in documentary making.

Core Requirements
Code
Title
Credits
Description
CSCI250
Introduction to
Programming
3
This course introduces the basic concepts and principles of structured programming in
Java. It starts with an introduction to Java, its syntax and the structure of a Java
program, and then covers simple data types, control structures, methods, arrays, and
strings.
CSCI250L
Introduction to
Programming Lab
1
This laboratory course is a corequisite of Introduction to Programming (CSCI250).
Students apply the programming fundamentals explained in CSCI250 by solving lab
exercises that use primitive data types, selection and repetition structures, methods,
and arrays. The lab gives students direct help from the instructor when needed; it is not
sufficient practice on its own, and students are expected to solve further exercises
independently.
MATH210
Calculus II
3
This is the second course in the Calculus sequence. The course material includes
logarithmic, exponential, and trigonometric functions, their inverses and their
derivatives, integration techniques, improper integrals, sequences, infinite series, tests
of convergence, alternating series, power series, polar coordinates and its application.
MATH220
Calculus III
3
The course extends the concepts of single-variable calculus to functions of several
variables and introduces vector calculus. Topics include vectors and geometry in space,
quadric surfaces, partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector fields, line and surface
integrals, and the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Greens and
Stokes Theorems.
MATH225
Linear Algebra with
Applications
3
Linear algebra provides a fundamental framework for representing and analyzing
mathematical problems that arise in many areas of science, engineering, economics, and
other disciplines. Many such problems can be expressed in terms of vectors, matrices,
and systems of linear equations, providing essential tools for their analysis and solution.
This course introduces the fundamental concepts of linear algebra and their
applications. The contents of this course include systems of linear equations, matrices
and determinants, vectors and vector spaces, linear transformations, linear
independence and bases, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and applications of linear
algebra.
MATH260
Discrete Mathematics
3
This course introduces discrete mathematical structures. Students will learn how to use
logical and mathematical formalisms to formulate and solve problems in computer
engineering. Topics include formal logic, proof techniques, recurrence relations, sets,
relations, functions, and algebraic structures.
MATH260L
Discrete Mathematics
Lab
1
This laboratory course provides guided practice in the fundamental concepts and
methods of discrete mathematics. Topics include logical statements and equivalences,
mathematical proofs using standard techniques and mathematical induction, set
operations, functions and countability through one-to-one correspondences, and
mathematical relations and ordered structures, including equivalence classes, partially
ordered sets, and lattices. Structured problem-solving activities help students apply
these concepts and methods to mathematical exercises.
MATH270
Ordinary Differential
Equations
3
Mathematical models for many of the basic laws of the physical sciences and, more
recently, of the biological and social sciences are formulated in terms of mathematical
equations involving certain known and unknown quantities and their derivatives. Such
equations are called differential equations. The study of differential equations is a vast
subject. This course introduces to ordinary differential equations and their applications.
The contents of this course include first order equations, separable, exact, and linear
equations, second and higher order differential equations, systems of differential
equations, series solutions, and Laplace transformation.
MATH310
Probability and
Statistics
3
The scope of this course is to provide a basic understanding of probability and statistics
for students. The topics include basic combinatorics, general probability rules, total and
Bayes probability theorems, probability distribution/density functions for
discrete/continuous random variables, expectation and variance of random variables,
covariance of two random variables, binomial and Poisson probability distributions,
Normal distribution, sampling distributions and central limit theorem, basic concept of
statistics, confidence intervals and hypothesis testing.
PHYS210
Mechanics
3
Develops a foundation in classical mechanics for science students through conceptual
lectures and collaborative problem solving. Topics include motion in one and two
dimensions, Newtons laws of motion, work and energy, linear momentum and
collisions, uniform and nonuniform circular motion, and the rotation of rigid bodies.
Students have the opportunity to build the mathematical and conceptual understanding
needed to analyze multi-body systems using the conservation of energy and of linear and
angular momentum.
PHYS250
Thermodynamics and
Waves
3
Develops a foundational understanding of oscillations, waves, sound, and
thermodynamics. Topics include simple harmonic motion, the propagation and
interference of mechanical waves, standing waves, the speed, frequency, and pressure
variations of sound, sound intensity and the decibel scale, the Doppler effect,
temperature, heat transfer, phase transitions, and the laws of thermodynamics.
Students have the opportunity to develop the analytical skills needed to solve physical
problems and to connect theoretical concepts with real-world applications.
PHYS280
Electricity &
Magnetism
3
Introduces calculus-based electromagnetism. Topics include electric forces and fields of
point charges and continuous charge distributions, Gausss law, electric potential,
capacitance, direct-current circuits and Kirchhoffs rules, magnetic forces and fields, the
BiotSavart and Ampre laws, Faradays and Lenzs laws, and an introduction to
Maxwells equations. Students have the opportunity to connect these topics to real-life
applications and to develop strategies for solving standard problems in
electromagnetism.
PHYS360
Analytical Mechanics
3
Provides an intermediate study of classical mechanics. After a review of vectors,
coordinate systems, and Newtonian mechanics, topics include position- and
velocity-dependent forces, projectile motion, free, damped, and forced oscillations,
noninertial reference frames, and the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formalisms,
including Hamiltons principle, generalized coordinates, and canonical equations.
Students have the opportunity to apply Newtonian and analytical methods to model and
analyze constrained mechanical systems.

Description
MATH305
Programming
Languages for
Scientists
3
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to scientific programming using
MATLAB, equipping students with the computational skills needed to solve
mathematical and physical problems. It covers fundamental programming concepts,
including variables, arrays, control flow, function creation, and data visualization.
Emphasis is placed on implementing numerical algorithms, developing efficient and
well-structured code, and using MATLABs built-in tools for linear algebra, polynomial
manipulation, and numerical computation. Through hands-on laboratory sessions,
students learn to translate mathematical formulations into executable programs and
interpret computational results. .
MATH315
Advanced Linear
Algebra
3
This course offers a rigorous study of linear algebra beyond the elementary level.
Emphasis is placed on abstract vector spaces, dimension and basis, inner product
spaces, orthogonality, eigenvalue theory, diagonalization, quadratic forms, and linear
transformations. The course develops proof-based reasoning together with
computational and numerical techniques, preparing students for advanced study and
applications in mathematics, physics, and engineering.
MATH330
Partial Differential
Equations
3
Partial differential equations are fundamental to mathematical modelling in science and
engineering and form a central area of applied analysis. This course introduces
analytical methods for standard first- and second-order partial differential equations.
Topics include quasi-linear equations and characteristics; classification and canonical
forms of second-order linear equations; Fourier series and separation of variables;
boundary-value problems for the wave, heat and Laplace equations; nonhomogeneous
problems; Fourier and Laplace transforms, including convolution and step and impulse
functions.
MATH345
Introduction to Real
Analysis
3
This course covers the fundamentals of mathematical analysis, including the algebraic,
order, and completeness properties of the real number system; sequences of real
numbers and their limits; limits of functions and their algebraic properties; and
continuity and differentiability. The course emphasizes the importance of abstract
concepts and develops students ability to understand and construct mathematical
proofs.
MATH365
Abstract Algebra
3
This course introduces the fundamental concepts and structures of group theory,
including groups, subgroups, cyclic and Abelian groups, permutation groups,
isomorphisms, cosets and Lagranges Theorem, normal subgroups and quotient groups,
group homomorphisms, direct products, and the Fundamental Theorem of Finite
Abelian Groups. Emphasis is placed on mathematical reasoning, proof construction,
problem solving, and the analysis of algebraic structures and relationships among
groups.
MATH375
Numerical Methods for
Scientists and
Engineers
3
Numerical analysis provides approximate solutions to mathematical problems for which
exact analytical solutions are unavailable or impractical. Students study the
mathematical concepts, computational techniques and algorithms behind numerical
methods, including root-finding, interpolation and polynomial approximation, numerical
differentiation and integration, extrapolation, and initial-value problems for first- and
higher-order ordinary differential equations. Emphasis is placed on the accuracy,
stability and efficiency of each method. Computer-based laboratory sessions in MATLAB
give students hands-on experience in turning mathematical algorithms into
computational procedures and applying them to mathematical and scientific problems.
MATH380
Complex Variables
3
This course provides an introduction to the theory and applications of functions of a
complex variable. Topics include complex numbers and their geometric representation,
analytic functions, limits, continuity, differentiation, and mappings. The course also
covers complex integration, Cauchys integral theorem and formula, Taylor and Laurent
series, zeros and singularities of complex functions, residues, the residue theorem, and
applications of complex analysis to the evaluation of integrals and related problems.
MATH385
Introduction to
Topology
3
This course introduces the fundamental concepts of topology, including topological
spaces, metric spaces, connectedness, and compactness.
MATH405
Number Theory
3
This course covers topics related to the theory of numbers. It aims to provide students
with a background in classical number theory and to introduce them to the divisibility of
integers, congruences, arithmetic functions, Diophantine equations, primitive roots,
second-order congruences, quadratic residues, the Legendre symbol, the Jacobi symbol,
and higher-order polynomial congruences. The course also familiarizes students with
the applications of number theory in computer science and cryptography.
MATH420
Differential Geometry
3
Differential Geometry is designed to introduce students to the geometric structure of
space or the universes geometry through the eyes of differential calculus. This course
aims to build a solid mathematical understanding of the fundamentals of differential
geometry with some intuition and visual appreciation of the given topics. It is essentially
based on the calculus of several variables. This course considers curves and surfaces in
Euclidean spaces, intrinsic properties, Frenet-Serret formulas, curvature, torsion, first
and second forms, geodesics, and extrinsic invariants of surfaces, First and Second
forms.
MATH455
Mathematical Analysis
3
Integration theory gives a rigorous framework for the area under a curve and its link to
continuity and differentiation. Students study the definition and properties of the
Riemann integral, criteria for Riemann integrability, classes of integrable functions, and
the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. The course then examines the limitations of the
Riemann integral and motivates the transition to Lebesgue measure and integration.
Students learn to construct rigorous arguments about integrability, explain the
relationship between differentiation and integration, and describe the basic principles of
Lebesgue integration.
MATH490
Modern Topics in
Algebra
3
This course is an introduction to ring and field theory. It covers polynomial rings over a
commutative ring, matrix rings, ideals and homomorphisms, quotient rings, Euclidean
domains, principal ideal domains, unique factorization domains, and field extensions.
MATH492
Mathematical Seminar
1
MATH492 is a one-credit seminar that prepares mathematics students for the Senior
Project by developing essential skills in scholarly communication and independent
learning. The course covers academic citation and referencing, mathematical report
writing, scientific typesetting with LaTeX or equivalent software, collaborative project
work, and the preparation of slide, oral, and poster presentations. Emphasis is placed on
clear mathematical exposition, appropriate notation, professional presentation design,
and confident communication of mathematical ideas.
Major Electives

Title
Credits
Description
MATH400
Special Functions
3
This course provides an in-depth study of special functions, which are important
mathematical tools in various areas of science and engineering. The course explores the
properties, applications, and techniques of the principal special functions, with a focus
on developing a solid understanding of their fundamental concepts and their use in
solving differential equations.
MATH460
Introduction to
Functional Analysis
3
Functional analysis is an abstract branch of mathematics that grew out of classical
analysis. Students study metric, normed, Banach, inner product and Hilbert spaces and
the fundamental theorems for normed and Banach spaces: the HahnBanach, uniform
boundedness, open mapping and closed graph theorems. Applications include the
Banach fixed point theorem, approximation theory, the spectral theory of linear
operators, and unbounded linear operators in quantum mechanics. Emphasis is placed
on applying these abstract concepts to concrete problems in mathematics and physics.
MATH465
Selected Topics In
Undergraduate
Mathematics
3
This course introduces elementary and advanced methods for solving Diophantine
equations, including classical equations, Pell-type equations, and applications of number
theory. It also covers recurrence relations, generating functions, characteristic roots,
and Fibonacci identities, emphasizing mathematical reasoning, problem-solving, and
rigorous proof techniques.
MATH495
Mathematics Senior
Project
3
This capstone course provides senior mathematics students with a structured transition
from theoretical study to independent mathematical research and professional practice.
Students develop research methodology, scientific writing, technical typesetting using
LaTeX or Scientific Word, literature review skills, ethical scholarship, and professional
presentation techniques. Each student completes an individual supervised research
project culminating in a formal written report and an oral defence using Beamer.
Collaborative applied activities are included to strengthen teamwork and
problem-solving skills.
General Education

Title
Credits
Description
ARAB200
Arabic Language and
Literature
3
This course develops critical knowledge and practical skills in Arabic language and
literature for non-specialists through three interconnected areas: literature, rhetoric,
and textual analysis; grammar, morphology, and spelling; and techniques of academic
and professional expression and communication. Students read texts from different
literary periods and schools, analyze their structure, ideas, and stylistic and rhetorical
features, and apply rules of grammar, morphology, and correct writing in the production
of coherent functional and academic texts. The course also develops the capacity for
responsible linguistic and cultural judgment and for accurate, informed use of Arabic in
university and professional contexts. Learning is assessed through attendance,
participation, classroom activities, the midterm examination, and the final examination.
CULT200
Introduction to
Arab-Islamic
Civilization
3
This course develops a critical understanding of the concept, formation, and interaction
of civilizations, with a focus on Arab-Islamic civilization in its historical, social,
intellectual, scientific, and artistic contexts. Students study examples of ancient
civilizations, the conditions of the Arabs before the prophetic mission, the foundations
and values of Arab-Islamic civilization, the experience of al-Andalus, and the
contributions of scholars and thinkers to history, geography, philosophy, medicine,
science, art, and architecture. They also analyze channels of interaction between East
and West and the effects of knowledge transfer, and develop the capacity for
responsible, evidence-based cultural judgment with respect for diversity and openness.
Learning is assessed through an analytical project, a comparative civilization task, the
midterm and final examinations, participation, and classroom activities.
ENGL201
Composition and
Research Skills
3
This course builds upon students previous knowledge of language and writing skills to
develop advanced academic composition, source-evaluation, and research-writing
competencies. Students engage with a variety of texts from different disciplines,
applying critical reading and research strategies to evaluate, integrate, and synthesize
information in their writing. The course emphasizes the composition of clear, coherent,
and well-supported academic essays through the effective use of rhetorical strategies,
academic language, and evidence from multiple sources. Students also develop
proficiency in summarizing, paraphrasing, synthesizing, and citing source material
accurately and ethically. Through guided practice, revision, and editing, students
strengthen their ability to communicate ideas effectively and independently in
research-based academic writing. Learning is assessed through written assessments,
midterm examination and final examination.
ENGL251
Communication Skills
3
ENGL251  Communication Skills prepares students to communicate clearly, ethically,
and professionally in contemporary academic and workplace contexts shaped by
artificial intelligence, digital platforms, hybrid work, and multicultural collaboration. In
the course, students study audience, purpose, tone, context, culture, and channel while
applying a three-phase writing process of planning, drafting, and revising. They practice
essential forms of workplace communication, including emails, memos, short digital
messages, positive and neutral messages, bad-news messages, persuasive and sales
messages, presentation materials, teamwork and meeting communication, rsums/CVs,
cover messages, interview responses, and follow-up messages. The course also teaches
students to evaluate and use AI tools responsibly as support for brainstorming, revision,
preparation, design awareness, rehearsal, and reflection without replacing human
judgment, accuracy, empathy, or academic integrity. Through lectures, discussion,
message analysis, writing workshops, peer review, presentations, and practical
assignments, students develop the communication competence needed for professional
credibility, career readiness, and ethical participation in AI-supported workplaces.

Physics Major Courses
Code
Title
Credits
Description
PHYS210
Mechanics
3
Develops a foundation in classical mechanics for science students through conceptual
lectures and collaborative problem solving. Topics include motion in one and two
dimensions, Newtons laws of motion, work and energy, linear momentum and
collisions, uniform and nonuniform circular motion, and the rotation of rigid bodies.
Students have the opportunity to build the mathematical and conceptual understanding
needed to analyze multi-body systems using the conservation of energy and of linear
and angular momentum.
PHYS250
Thermodynamics and
Waves
3
Develops a foundational understanding of oscillations, waves, sound, and
thermodynamics. Topics include simple harmonic motion, the propagation and
interference of mechanical waves, standing waves, the speed, frequency, and pressure
variations of sound, sound intensity and the decibel scale, the Doppler effect,
temperature, heat transfer, phase transitions, and the laws of thermodynamics.
Students have the opportunity to develop the analytical skills needed to solve physical
problems and to connect theoretical concepts with real-world applications.
PHYS280
Electricity &
Magnetism
3
Introduces calculus-based electromagnetism. Topics include electric forces and fields
of point charges and continuous charge distributions, Gausss law, electric potential,
capacitance, direct-current circuits and Kirchhoffs rules, magnetic forces and fields,
the BiotSavart and Ampre laws, Faradays and Lenzs laws, and an introduction to
Maxwells equations. Students have the opportunity to connect these topics to real-life
applications and to develop strategies for solving standard problems in
electromagnetism.
PHYS300
Mathematical Physics
3
Introduces the mathematical techniques used across physics. Topics include vector
calculus in Cartesian and curvilinear coordinates with the divergence and Stokes
theorems, matrix methods and eigenvalue problems, functions of a complex variable
and analytic functions, the Dirac delta function, and Fourier series and transforms.
Students have the opportunity to apply these methods to problems from different
branches of physics.
PHYS330
Electromagnetic Fields
and Waves I
3
Develops electrostatics at the intermediate level. Topics include the electric field and
potential of charge distributions using Coulombs and Gausss laws, the work and
energy of discrete and continuous charge distributions, conductors and capacitors, the
solution of Laplaces equation by separation of variables and by the method of images,
multipole expansion, and the field of an electric dipole. Students have the opportunity
to apply these tools to describe the polarization, the displacement vector, and the
dielectric constant of linear dielectric materials.
PHYS340
Modern Physics
3
Introduces special relativity and the foundations of quantum physics. Topics include
the special theory of relativity, relativistic momentum and energy, the quantum theory
of light, the particle nature of matter, matter waves, quantum mechanics in one
dimension, and tunneling phenomena. Students apply these concepts to solve problems
in relativistic and quantum physics.
PHYS350
Physical Optics
3
Introduces the fundamental principles of optics through ray and wave descriptions of
light. Topics include reflection and refraction, image formation with lenses and
mirrors, the wave and electromagnetic nature of light, light propagation in dielectric
media, interference and coherence, and Fraunhofer diffraction. Students have the
opportunity to apply these principles to analyze optical phenomena and to solve
problems on the propagation and behavior of light.
PHYS360
Analytical Mechanics
3
Provides an intermediate study of classical mechanics. After a review of vectors,
coordinate systems, and Newtonian mechanics, topics include position- and
velocity-dependent forces, projectile motion, free, damped, and forced oscillations,
noninertial reference frames, and the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formalisms,
including Hamiltons principle, generalized coordinates, and canonical equations.
Students have the opportunity to apply Newtonian and analytical methods to model
and analyze constrained mechanical systems.
PHYS380
Electromagnetic Fields
and Waves II
3
Develops magnetostatics and electrodynamics at the intermediate level, culminating in
Maxwells equations. Topics include the Lorentz force law, the BiotSavart law, the
divergence and curl of the magnetic field, Ampres law, the magnetic vector potential,
magnetization and bound currents, the auxiliary field H and magnetic susceptibility,
electromotive force, Faradays and Lenzs laws, inductance and magnetic energy, and
the displacement current. Students apply vector-calculus methods to solve standard
problems in magnetism and electromagnetic induction.
PHYS420
Quantum Mechanics
3
Introduces the basic principles of quantum mechanics. Topics include the wave
function and its statistical interpretation, normalization, momentum, the uncertainty
principle, and the time-independent Schrdinger equation for the stationary states of
the infinite square well, the harmonic oscillator, the free particle, the delta-function
potential, and the finite square well. Students also have the opportunity to learn the
mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics, using Dirac notation for observables
and Hermitian operators in Hilbert space, and the generalized statistical
interpretation.
PHYS430
Thermal Physics I
3
Develops classical thermodynamics from the macroscopic point of view. Topics include
temperature and the zeroth law, equations of state of ideal and real gases, work and
heat, the first and second laws of thermodynamics, the Carnot cycle and heat engines,
entropy and the principle of increase of entropy, pure substances and phase diagrams,
and the characteristic functions and Maxwells relations. The course prepares students
for statistical physics.
PHYS450
Solid State Physics
3
Introduces the physics of crystalline solids. Topics include crystal structures in two and
three dimensions, Bravais lattices, Miller indices, the reciprocal lattice, and the
determination of crystal structure by X-ray diffraction using Braggs law and the Laue
formulation. Lattice vibrations are treated as elastic waves in monatomic and diatomic
crystals, and the Einstein and Debye models are used to explain heat capacity, thermal
expansion, and thermal conductivity. Students also have the opportunity to study the
free-electron Fermi gas model and its application to the electronic heat capacity and
the electrical and thermal conductivity of metals.
PHYS470
Advanced Quantum
Mechanics
3
Continues the introduction to quantum mechanics. Topics include the mathematical
structure of quantum mechanics, the time-independent Schrdinger equation in three
dimensions and the hydrogen atom, orbital and spin angular momentum, the addition
of angular momenta, and systems of identical particles. Students have the opportunity
to apply advanced mathematical techniques to three-dimensional and multi-particle
quantum systems.
PHYS480
Thermal Physics II
3
Complements Thermal Physics I with statistical mechanics. Topics include distribution
functions, MaxwellBoltzmann, FermiDirac, and BoseEinstein statistics, black-body
radiation, the partition function, the heat capacity of solids, and BoseEinstein and
FermiDirac gases, with applications to monatomic and diatomic ideal gases. Students
have the opportunity to relate the microscopic and macroscopic properties of physical
systems.
PHYS490
Physics Seminar
1
Offers students the opportunity to explore independently a selected physics topic
beyond the scope of the core curriculum. Students prepare a research-based report
and presentation, and have the opportunity to develop skills in literature review,
critical analysis, scientific writing, and oral communication, to discuss and defend
scientific ideas, and to evaluate the work of their peers.
Physics Labs
Code
Title
Credits
Description
PHYS250L
Thermodynamics and
Waves Lab
1
Introduces the experimental techniques used to study oscillations, wave motion, and
thermodynamics. Experiments cover Hookes law, the simple pendulum and simple
harmonic motion, Archimedes principle, standing waves and the speed of sound, the
mechanical equivalent of heat, the specific heat and heat capacity of metals, and
thermal conductivity. Students have the opportunity to apply error analysis, to
compare experimental results with theoretical predictions, and to write clear
laboratory reports.
PHYS280L
Electricity and
Magnetism Lab
1
Reinforces the concepts of electricity and magnetism through hands-on experiments.
Students verify Ohms law for a resistor, a capacitor, and a coil; study the grouping of
resistors, RL circuits, and the charging and discharging of a capacitor; investigate the
variation of resistance with temperature and the resistivity of a metal by the
four-terminal method; and study resonance in a series RLC circuit, the magnetic field
inside a solenoid, and the transformer. Students have the opportunity to build and
diagram circuits, to read analogue and digital instruments and the oscilloscope, to
estimate and propagate measurement uncertainties, to fit straight-line graphs by least
squares, and to relate their results to Kirchhoffs, Ampres, and Faradays laws.
PHYS340L
Atomic Physics Lab
1
Provides hands-on experience of the experimental foundations of modern physics,
primarily atomic physics, and of the relationship between experiment and theory.
Experiments include the specific charge of the electron, the Millikan oil-drop
experiment, electron absorption, the photoelectric effect, atomic emission spectra and
the Rydberg constant, the FranckHertz experiment, and electron diffraction. Students
have the opportunity to examine the dual nature of light and particles and the
quantization of atomic energy levels, and to report their results with a proper
treatment of uncertainties.
PHYS350L
Physical Optics Lab
1
Familiarizes students with historically important optical experiments and with modern
optical instruments and methods. Students apply the laws of geometrical optics,
including refraction, total internal reflection, lenses, and prisms, and investigate
physical optics, including interference, diffraction, and interferometry, using a He-Ne
laser and other optical equipment. Students have the opportunity to develop an
understanding of the nature of light and of the concepts behind modern optical
technology, and to report their measurements with a proper treatment of uncertainties.
Supporting Courses

Title
Credits
Description
CHEM200
General Chemistry
3
This course is designed for students who wish to acquire the basic principles of
chemistry. The emphasis of the course will be on the fundamental principles of general
chemistry, which include terminology, qualitative concepts and quantitative skills. The
general topics included in this course are: Quantum Theory of the Atom; Electrons and
Periodicity; Bonding; Molecular Geometry; Hybridization; Acid-base Chemistry;
equilibrium and Kinetics.
CSCI250
Introduction to
Programming
3
This course introduces the basic concepts and principles of structured programming in
Java. It starts with an introduction to Java, its syntax and the structure of a Java
program, and then covers simple data types, control structures, methods, arrays, and
strings.
CSCI250L
Introduction to
Programming Lab
1
This laboratory course is a corequisite of Introduction to Programming (CSCI250).
Students apply the programming fundamentals explained in CSCI250 by solving lab
exercises that use primitive data types, selection and repetition structures, methods,
and arrays. The lab gives students direct help from the instructor when needed; it is
not sufficient practice on its own, and students are expected to solve further exercises
independently.
MATH210
Calculus II
3
This is the second course in the Calculus sequence. The course material includes
logarithmic, exponential, and trigonometric functions, their inverses and their
derivatives, integration techniques, improper integrals, sequences, infinite series, tests
of convergence, alternating series, power series, polar coordinates and its application.
MATH220
Calculus III
3
The course extends the concepts of single-variable calculus to functions of several
variables and introduces vector calculus. Topics include vectors and geometry in
space, quadric surfaces, partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector fields, line and
surface integrals, and the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Greens
and Stokes Theorems.
MATH225
Linear Algebra with
Applications
3
Linear algebra provides a fundamental framework for representing and analyzing
mathematical problems that arise in many areas of science, engineering, economics,
and other disciplines. Many such problems can be expressed in terms of vectors,
matrices, and systems of linear equations, providing essential tools for their analysis
and solution. This course introduces the fundamental concepts of linear algebra and
their applications. The contents of this course include systems of linear equations,
matrices and determinants, vectors and vector spaces, linear transformations, linear
independence and bases, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and applications of linear
algebra.
MATH270
Ordinary Differential
Equations
3
Mathematical models for many of the basic laws of the physical sciences and, more
recently, of the biological and social sciences are formulated in terms of mathematical
equations involving certain known and unknown quantities and their derivatives. Such
equations are called differential equations. The study of differential equations is a vast
subject. This course introduces to ordinary differential equations and their
applications. The contents of this course include first order equations, separable, exact,
and linear equations, second and higher order differential equations, systems of
differential equations, series solutions, and Laplace transformation.
MATH305
Programming
Languages for
Scientists
3
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to scientific programming using
MATLAB, equipping students with the computational skills needed to solve
mathematical and physical problems. It covers fundamental programming concepts,
including variables, arrays, control flow, function creation, and data visualization.
Emphasis is placed on implementing numerical algorithms, developing efficient and
well-structured code, and using MATLABs built-in tools for linear algebra, polynomial
manipulation, and numerical computation. Through hands-on laboratory sessions,
students learn to translate mathematical formulations into executable programs and
interpret computational results. .
MATH375
Numerical Methods for
Scientists and
Engineers
3
Numerical analysis provides approximate solutions to mathematical problems for
which exact analytical solutions are unavailable or impractical. Students study the
mathematical concepts, computational techniques and algorithms behind numerical
methods, including root-finding, interpolation and polynomial approximation,
numerical differentiation and integration, extrapolation, and initial-value problems for
first- and higher-order ordinary differential equations. Emphasis is placed on the
accuracy, stability and efficiency of each method. Computer-based laboratory sessions
in MATLAB give students hands-on experience in turning mathematical algorithms into
computational procedures and applying them to mathematical and scientific problems.

Code
Title
Credits
Description
EDUC253
Technology
Integration in
Education
3
How can educators thoughtfully incorporate technology to boost student achievement
and engagement? This course examines the evolving role of technology in the
classroom, focusing on technology-enhanced instruction, digital tools for differentiated
learning, and recent innovations in educational technology. Through experiential
learning, collaborative projects, and case-based analysis, students connect theory to
practice by integrating digital tools into authentic educational contexts. By the end of
the course, learners will be equipped to choose and implement appropriate
technologies across diverse educational settings and to design learner-centered,
technology-supported lessons that foster engagement and academic success.
PHYS370
Nuclear Physics
3
Introduces the physics of the atomic nucleus and of elementary particles. Topics
include the basic properties of nuclei, the liquid drop and nuclear shell models,
radioactive decay and its applications, nuclear reactions, fission and fusion, and the
fundamental forces, quarks, and the Standard Model. Students have the opportunity to
apply conservation laws and nuclear models to quantitative problems.
PHYS495
Physics Senior Project
3
Gives senior physics students the opportunity to plan, carry out, and report an
independent project under faculty supervision. Students select an experimental,
computational, or theoretical topic, review the scientific literature critically, and
formulate a well-defined research question with a realistic work plan. They carry out
the project, keep accurate records, analyze data with an appropriate treatment of
uncertainties, and compare their results with theoretical predictions. Through
seminars, workshops, and regular supervisor meetings, students have the opportunity
to develop skills in scientific writing, oral presentation, project management, and
research ethics. The course culminates in a written report and an oral defense that
integrate the knowledge and skills acquired throughout the physics program.

Title
Credits
Description
ARAB200
Arabic Language and
Literature
3
This course develops critical knowledge and practical skills in Arabic language and
literature for non-specialists through three interconnected areas: literature, rhetoric,
and textual analysis; grammar, morphology, and spelling; and techniques of academic
and professional expression and communication. Students read texts from different
literary periods and schools, analyze their structure, ideas, and stylistic and rhetorical
features, and apply rules of grammar, morphology, and correct writing in the
production of coherent functional and academic texts. The course also develops the
capacity for responsible linguistic and cultural judgment and for accurate, informed
use of Arabic in university and professional contexts. Learning is assessed through
attendance, participation, classroom activities, the midterm examination, and the final
examination.
CULT200
Introduction to
Arab-Islamic
Civilization
3
This course develops a critical understanding of the concept, formation, and
interaction of civilizations, with a focus on Arab-Islamic civilization in its historical,
social, intellectual, scientific, and artistic contexts. Students study examples of ancient
civilizations, the conditions of the Arabs before the prophetic mission, the foundations
and values of Arab-Islamic civilization, the experience of al-Andalus, and the
contributions of scholars and thinkers to history, geography, philosophy, medicine,
science, art, and architecture. They also analyze channels of interaction between East
and West and the effects of knowledge transfer, and develop the capacity for
responsible, evidence-based cultural judgment with respect for diversity and openness.
Learning is assessed through an analytical project, a comparative civilization task, the
midterm and final examinations, participation, and classroom activities.
ENGL201
Composition and
Research Skills
3
This course builds upon students previous knowledge of language and writing skills to
develop advanced academic composition, source-evaluation, and research-writing
competencies. Students engage with a variety of texts from different disciplines,
applying critical reading and research strategies to evaluate, integrate, and synthesize
information in their writing. The course emphasizes the composition of clear, coherent,
and well-supported academic essays through the effective use of rhetorical strategies,
academic language, and evidence from multiple sources. Students also develop
proficiency in summarizing, paraphrasing, synthesizing, and citing source material
accurately and ethically. Through guided practice, revision, and editing, students
strengthen their ability to communicate ideas effectively and independently in
research-based academic writing. Learning is assessed through written assessments,
midterm examination and final examination.
ENGL251
Communication Skills
3
ENGL251  Communication Skills prepares students to communicate clearly, ethically,
and professionally in contemporary academic and workplace contexts shaped by
artificial intelligence, digital platforms, hybrid work, and multicultural collaboration. In
the course, students study audience, purpose, tone, context, culture, and channel while
applying a three-phase writing process of planning, drafting, and revising. They
practice essential forms of workplace communication, including emails, memos, short
digital messages, positive and neutral messages, bad-news messages, persuasive and
sales messages, presentation materials, teamwork and meeting communication,
rsums/CVs, cover messages, interview responses, and follow-up messages. The
course also teaches students to evaluate and use AI tools responsibly as support for
brainstorming, revision, preparation, design awareness, rehearsal, and reflection
without replacing human judgment, accuracy, empathy, or academic integrity. Through
lectures, discussion, message analysis, writing workshops, peer review, presentations,
and practical assignments, students develop the communication competence needed
for professional credibility, career readiness, and ethical participation in AI-supported
workplaces.

Core Requirements

Title

Description
ADVR300
Advertising Theory &
Practice
3
Advertising Theory and Practice provides a comprehensive overview on Advertising, its
role in building a brands image and brand equity, its diverse techniques used to
influence people's mind by satisfying or creating consumers needs, its communicational
impact on society that keeps on generating trends as well as its persuasive force in
increasing sales and encouraging consumers to make the purchase. Broad attention is
given to key subjects such as advertising agency practices, branding, media planning,
creative and marketing strategies.
ARTS350
Photography
3
Photography is addressed to all students who wish to learn about digital photography
basics, eventually, how to use a digital camera and lenses. Students will learn terms and
theory using manual techniques in a digital single lens reflex camera. This course
involves the power of images through image language, composition and philosophy. It
covers as well the use of the digital dark room for the enhancement of ideas, products
and /or creative necessity. It leads students towards a deeper understanding of light,
key value, equipment and camera controls
COMM200
Introduction to
Communication
Studies
3
Introduction to Mass Communication introduces students to the central concepts of
image theories in communication and the operation of the media industries. It is an
introduction to the history, structure, process and social environment of each medium in
the communication industry; an overview of the emerging technology in mass media and
its social impact. It is a study of the development, principles and effects of Print, Public
Relations, Advertising, Radio, TV, film and Computer/Online-Generated communication.
Particular attention will be given to the study of different types of mass and interactive
media and how they function in modern society. It reviews the historical and regulatory
bases of the media along with their social implications.
COMM220
Rhetoric & Persuasion
3
Rhetoric and Persuasion provides students with the foundation to understand the
definition of key terms, offering a retrospective glance to the historical foundations of
rhetoric and persuasion. It provides insights on important considerations of the
persuasion on the social through rhetoric. It provides a model for professional practice
focusing on developing skills in critical self-reflection, as well as professional
persuasion.
COMM225
Workshop
3
Workshop I is an entry-level course that will introduce students to the fundamentals of
video making. Students will learn to use video and sound as an effective form of
communication, and will learn how to successfully utilize those elements separately and
simultaneously, to be able to transform an idea into a persuasive story.
COMM265
Performance Theory &
Practice
3
Performance Theory and Practice introduces students to the ambiguity that lies in trying
to define what performance as a discipline might mean, which makes this course very
challenging. It is very essential to note that performance in not theatre, without
neglecting the fact that performing is a part of acting. The subject in action is not an
actor; he is only experiencing a new game where others, as subjects (physical and
emotional) are taking part in this game. What comes out of this game is what will
mark the journey of each and every subject involved in this class. It is not a theatre
course, but it involves character games, breathing techniques, mediation and a rough
body work. And because the discipline is still under construction all around the world,
the game is set between the students and the facilitator. Hence, the facilitator i.e.
the instructor is part of the game. It is all about a behavior in front of an audience.
COMM285
Theories of Perception
3
Theories of Perception is an introductory course on communication languages and
perception modes in relation to the technology of image production. It is an
investigation of the semiotics of representation and perception throughout different
medium usage and major art and media movements. It also covers the development of
image theories and representation toward the various elements of communication and
throughout history in relation to technology as a major variable for the image
production.
COMM305
Artificial Intelligence
and Mass Media
3
This course provides an in-depth exploration of the intersection between artificial
intelligence (AI) and mass media. It examines how AI technologies are transforming
media production, distribution, and consumption. Students will analyze the ethical
implications, the impact on journalism, advertising, and public relations, and the role of
AI in shaping societal narratives.
GDES270
Design Software I
3
Design software 1 introduces students to aiding software for Graphic Design. Using the
Adobe suite, Adobe Illustrator plays a significant role in graphic design. As a vector
oriented software, illustrator opens a gateway of opportunities for a graphic designer to
work with ease in implementing the essential work for print, web and other media.
Adobe InDesign complements Illustrator at producing multiple page content instead of
art boards and by that, playing an essential role at strengthening sense of layout and
identity. Adobe Photoshop plays a major role in photo editing. Accompanied by Adobe
illustrator, these 2 software manage to create most demanding projects especially that
of print. The student will have the opportunity to learn and practice the essentials in
these software. Keeping the sketchbook to bring up ideas to life, the designated
software shall add ease and speed rather than the long timed labor of manual work.
JORN285
Travel Journalism
3
Travel Journalism provides students with the foundation to understand the setting of the
fundamental writing skills required by freelance writers.  It exposes students to the
experience and savoir-faire of successful travel writing. Flexible in its approach, the
course teaches the craft of creating travel media through writing and photography,
covering diverse topics of journalism and blogging. The objective is to address markets
needs through building skills in the chosen medium and creating and marketing the
writers personal brand.
PREL300
Public Relations
Principles & Concepts
3
Public Relations Principles and Concept introduces students to the basic principles of
public relations. In this course, students will learn how to identify the main concepts
and principles in the field of public relations, which will further be elaborated on, in
subsequent courses. The course will also provide students with the knowledge to
practice the basics of PR

CSCI200
Introduction to
Computers
3
This course introduces students to the fundamental concepts of computer science and
technology, with a focus on practical applications and interactive learning. Designed for
Generation Z students pursuing degrees in basic Education in  English, Math, or
Science, the course emphasizes hands-on experience, critical thinking, and the use of
modern tools and platforms. The  philosophy centers around fostering digital literacy
and responsible use of technology, recognizing the importance of equipping future
educators and professionals with essential tech skills. By the end of the course, students
will be proficient in using common software applications, understand basic computer
hardware and operating systems, and apply problem-solving skills to real-world
scenarios using computer tools. The impact of this course extends beyond technical
proficiency, as it aims to develop students' ability to navigate the digital world
effectively, enhance their educational and professional opportunities, and promote a
culture of continuous learning and adaptation in a rapidly evolving technological
landscape.
CULT200
Introduction to Arab -
Islamic Civilization
3
This course delves into the intellectual and cultural achievements of Arab-Islamic
civilization, aiming to expose students to the significant contributions made by Arab
scholars in science, philosophy, literature, and the arts. Rooted in the philosophy that
open-minded inquiry fuels intellectual advancement, the course emphasizes the holistic
and curious approach of historical Arab scholars who transcended dogmatic limitations.
Through exploring these achievements, students will gain a broader perspective on the
development of global knowledge, recognizing the pivotal role of Arab-Islamic
civilization in connecting ancient and medieval worlds. By the end of the course,
students will appreciate the interconnectedness of human knowledge and be inspired to
adopt a spirit of curiosity and respect for diverse intellectual traditions in their pursuits.
The medium of instruction is in both English and Arabic.
ENGL201
Composition and
Research Skills
3
Welcome to the next step in your academic writing journey! This course marks an
advancement in students' academic writing development, focusing on the fundamental
skills of summarizing, paraphrasing, and synthesizing information. Building upon prior
English Language knowledge, the course aims to enhance students' critical thinking and
academic writing competencies. Students will engage with a diverse range of texts from
various disciplines, developing effective strategies for responding to and integrating
these sources within their written work. Through practical application, students will
focus on composing different essay forms, while also refining their ability to construct
clear, grammatically correct sentences and expanding their academic vocabulary and
diction. Upon completion of this course, students will be well-prepared to produce
thoroughly researched and synthesized essays, demonstrating their proficiency in
advanced academic writing.
ENGL251
Communication Skills
3
Thriving in todays fast-paced, digitally connected professional world requires strong
and adaptable communication abilities, making ENGL251  English Communication
Skills  an essential foundation for career readiness. This course aims to develop
students mastery of key principles and strategies that underpin effective
communication across various professional scenarios. Rooted in the belief that
communication proficiency grows through both conceptual understanding and hands-on
practice, the course blends focused instruction with applied, real-world tasks. Students
will explore audience awareness and message design using the 3-X-3 writing process as
a framework for producing clear, purposeful communication. They will engage with
topics such as crafting persuasive and tactful negative messages, communicating
professionally in face-to-face settings, and enhancing their employability through the
creation of persuasive rsums, cover letters, and strong interview performance.
Through a mix of lectures, collaborative discussions, practical exercises, and digital
writing assignments, the course fosters an active and participatory classroom
environment. Assessment methods include quizzes, a midterm and final exam, as well as
targeted business writing tasks, ensuring students are evaluated on both theoretical
insight and real-world application. By the end of ENGL251, students will be
well-equipped to communicate confidently and effectively in a variety of digital and
professional settings. They will be able to tailor their messages to diverse audiences,
engage in collaborative communication, and use their English language skills
strategically to succeed in the modern workplace.
